lessons.title: Structural Loads in Layered Food
lessons.content: A sandwich is a load-bearing structure and most failures are structural rather than culinary. The bottom slice carries the entire compressive load of every layer above it. When the bottom slice absorbs moisture its compressive strength falls sharply, which engineers call sogginess failure. The standard mitigation is a moisture barrier, usually a fat layer such as butter or mayonnaise applied to the inner face of each slice. A second common failure is lateral slip, where layers slide relative to one another under shear. Lettuce is the usual culprit because its surface has a very low coefficient of friction when wet. Placing a high friction layer such as cheese directly beneath the lettuce reduces slip considerably.

lessons.title: Thermal Management
lessons.content: Heat moves through a sandwich mainly by conduction, and the layers have very different thermal conductivities. A hot filling placed directly against bread will drive moisture into the bread and cause sogginess failure within minutes. The recommended practice is to allow hot fillings to cool to below sixty degrees Celsius before assembly, or to insulate the filling from the bread with a low conductivity layer. Cheese is a poor thermal insulator but an excellent moisture barrier, so it is usually placed against the bread rather than against the filling. Toasting the bread increases its stiffness and reduces its permeability, which is why toasted sandwiches tolerate wet fillings better.

lessons.title: Failure Analysis and Case Studies
lessons.content: Post-failure analysis of a sandwich follows the same discipline as any other engineering investigation. Identify the failure mode first, then the immediate cause, then the design decision that permitted it. The three dominant modes are sogginess failure, lateral slip, and catastrophic filling ejection, where compressive load exceeds the friction holding the filling in place and the contents are expelled sideways. Ejection is almost always a loading problem rather than a materials problem, and the fix is to reduce fill height rather than to change ingredients. Documenting failures in a shared log is strongly encouraged, since the same three modes recur constantly.

lessons.title: Message Encoding and Payload Limits
lessons.content: A carrier pigeon has a practical payload of around seventy five grams, which in paper terms is roughly ten sheets. Messages must therefore be encoded compactly. The traditional approach is a fixed field format where each field has a known position and length, so no delimiters are needed. Compression helps but has an important caveat: a corrupted compressed message is usually unrecoverable in full, whereas a corrupted fixed field message loses only the damaged field. For this reason critical messages are sent uncompressed and redundantly, on two birds, rather than compressed on one.

lessons.title: Routing and Delivery Guarantees
lessons.content: Pigeon routing offers at-most-once delivery and no acknowledgement. The bird either arrives or it does not, and the sender learns nothing either way. Systems built on pigeon transport therefore cannot assume delivery and must either tolerate loss or build acknowledgement out of a second bird flying the reverse route. Latency is highly variable, ranging from forty minutes to several days depending on weather, predation and the bird's own judgement. Designers should treat the transport as eventually consistent at best, and should never use it for anything requiring ordering between messages, since two birds released together routinely arrive days apart.

lessons.title: Security Considerations
lessons.content: A pigeon is an unauthenticated transport. Anyone who intercepts the bird can read the message, alter it, and release the bird to continue its journey, and the recipient has no way to detect this. Encryption of the payload is the only real protection, and it must be done before the message is attached. Physical security of the loft matters more than most operators expect, because an attacker who gains access to the loft can substitute their own birds and receive all future traffic. Signs of compromise include unfamiliar birds, and messages arriving substantially faster than the route normally allows.

lessons.title: Scoring and Judging Criteria
lessons.content: Competitive napping is scored across three categories. Onset speed measures the time from the start signal to verified sleep, and is worth forty percent. Depth measures how far the napper descends through the sleep stages within the allotted twenty minutes, and is worth forty percent. Recovery measures how alert the napper is sixty seconds after being woken, and is worth the remaining twenty percent. Competitors frequently over-optimise for depth and lose more points on recovery than they gain, because deep sleep produces significant grogginess on waking. The highest scoring strategy is usually a fast onset to a moderate depth.

lessons.title: Environmental Controls
lessons.content: Ambient temperature is the single largest controllable factor in onset speed. Body temperature must fall for sleep onset to occur, so a cool room accelerates onset while a warm room delays it substantially. The competitive range is sixteen to eighteen degrees Celsius. Light matters less than most competitors assume provided an eye mask is used, but sound matters a great deal, and intermittent noise is far more disruptive than steady noise of the same volume. Many competitors use steady broadband noise to mask intermittent sounds rather than attempting silence, which is rarely achievable in a competition hall.

lessons.title: Training Regimes and Common Injuries
lessons.content: Onset speed responds well to conditioning, and most competitors train by napping at exactly the same time daily to establish a circadian anchor. Depth responds poorly to training and is largely constitutional. The most common competitive injury is not physical but circadian: aggressive training schedules desynchronise the competitor's body clock, producing chronic insomnia that ends careers. Coaches now generally cap training at one nap per day and mandate rest weeks. A secondary injury is neck strain from poor positioning, which is straightforward to prevent with proper support but accounts for a surprising share of withdrawals.
